analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and funds them with new taxes on high earners and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it received no vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise every Social Security benefit, growing to 15% higher over time, change cost-of-living adjustments to an inflation index that tracks what seniors actually buy, and lift lifetime low earners' minimum benefits up to the poverty line. It would pay for this by collecting Social Security payroll tax on wages above $250,000 — wages that are currently exempt — and raising the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 10%. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: All current and future Social Security beneficiaries get an across-the-board increase reaching 15% by 2037. Retirees get more accurate cost-of-living adjustments under an index that tracks seniors' spending, especially on health care. Lifetime low earners get a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line, rising with each year of work. The program's trust funds get dedicated new revenue for solvency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees, disabled beneficiaries, low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises every beneficiary's benefit amount by 1% per year starting in 2023, reaching 15% higher by 2037 [S2] [S3].
Switches cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the spending patterns of older households, including higher health care costs [S2] [S3].

Guarantees a minimum benefit for lifetime low earners based on a share of the poverty guideline, scaled from 6.25% at 11 years of work to 125% at 30 or more years, and recomputes benefits for those already retired [S3].

Funds the expansion by making wages above $250,000 subject to Social Security payroll tax — closing the cap that currently exempts all earnings above the annual wage base — and by raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10%, with the revenue directed to the Old-Age and Disability trust funds [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-income earners who make over $250,000 a year pay Social Security tax on their excess wages. Wealthy households with investment income pay a sharply higher tax, 10% instead of 3.8%, on net investment gains.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and investors with investment income

drawbacks.text: Employers and high-income self-employed workers face the added payroll tax above $250,000, which could reduce hiring or shift pay toward untaxed forms of compensation for top earners [S3].

The higher investment income tax could reduce after-tax returns for savers and retirees who have investment income, not only the very wealthy, since the 3.8% tax it replaces applies broadly to households above certain income thresholds.

The bill as introduced had no provisions addressing the taxpayer cost concerns that usually accompany benefit expansions; its solvency case rests entirely on the new taxes producing the projected revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most retirees and disabled beneficiaries the gains are direct and immediate: bigger checks, a more accurate inflation adjustment, and a poverty-level floor for the lowest earners. The costs fall on a narrow group — wage earners above $250,000 and households with significant investment income. The main design risk is that the financing depends on projections of the new tax revenue holding up; the bill provides no fallback if they fall short.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on February 16, 2017, joined by Senator Gillibrand as an original cosponsor [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day [S5].
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action of any kind was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and wealthy households with investment income kept the current tax structure: no payroll tax on wages above $250,000 and the 3.8% investment income tax stayed in place. Social Security beneficiaries got no benefit increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors kept existing tax rates

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security and payroll tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the referral was the last action of record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent senator who votes with Democrats, and all four cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee chaired by a Republican without a hearing or vote [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: High-income wage earners and their employers
industries.note: The bill extends Social Security payroll tax to every dollar of wages above $250,000, which is currently untaxed. The added cost lands on employees and employers at the top of the pay scale, while the revenue funds higher benefits for ordinary beneficiaries.

The net investment income tax nearly triples, from 3.8% to 10%, with the proceeds dedicated to the Social Security trust funds. Wealthy households bear most of this because investment income is concentrated at the top.
